title: aussie
chapters: How a new accent was born

units.t: Aussie English, Explained.
Part one. How a new accent was born.
If you've ever had a mate say they'll swing by the servo this arvo, you've heard one of the most distinctive varieties of English in the world.
In this lesson, we'll look at where Australian English came from, why it loves shortening words, and the stories behind a few of its most famous expressions.
Let's start at the beginning.
When the First Fleet arrived in 1788, it brought people from all over Britain and Ireland.
There were Londoners, people from the south east of England, people from the north, and, once convict ships began arriving from Ireland in 1791, a large number of Irish.
Each group had its own accent and its own local words.
Their children, though, grew up together.
Kids pick up language mostly from other kids, and in the colony, they were hearing a mix of all those accents at once.
Over a generation or two, the mix settled into something new.
Linguists call this process levelling, where lots of different dialects blend into a shared one.
Visitors to the colony were remarking that the locally born children sounded different from their parents as early as the 1820s.
There are plenty of popular myths about the Australian accent.
One says Australians talk through half-closed lips to keep the flies out.
Another says the early settlers were so often drunk that their slurred speech became the national accent.
That second idea got a lot of media attention in 2015, but linguists were quick to reject it.
There's no evidence for either theory.
The accent came from mixing, not from flies or rum.
Australians have also always enjoyed poking fun at their own speech.
In 1965, a book called Let Stalk Strine was published under the pen name Afferbeck Lauder.
Say that name out loud, and you'll hear alphabetical order.
The author was actually an artist called Alastair Morrison, and the title, of course, means let's talk Australian.
His word Strine is still used today as a cheeky name for broad Australian English.
Broad is actually a technical term here.
In the 1960s, two linguists, Alexander Mitchell and Arthur Delbridge, recorded thousands of Australian high school students.
They sorted the accents they heard into three broad groups.
Broad, like a classic outback character, general, which most Australians speak, and cultivated, which sounds closer to British English.
Since then, the cultivated accent has become much rarer, and general Australian is by far the most common.
One more surprising thing is how similar the accent is across such a huge country.
Someone from Perth and someone from Brisbane live more than three and a half thousand kilometres apart, yet they sound remarkably alike.
There are small differences, though.
For example, people in Adelaide are much more likely to say dahnce, while in most other cities, dance with a short A, as in ant, is more common.
Part two. Why Australians shorten words.
Our first word is arvo.
A, R, V, O.
Here's an everyday example.
Are you free this arvo, or should we catch up on the weekend?
Arvo simply means afternoon.
And our second word is its close cousin, servo.
S, E, R, V, O.
For example, I'll grab milk from the servo on the way home.
A servo is a service station, or what some other countries call a petrol station or gas station.
These words are part of a huge family.
Linguists call them hypocoristics, which is a technical name for shortened, familiar forms of words.
Australian English is famous for them.
Some end in O, like arvo, servo, ambo for an ambulance officer, rego for your car registration, and bottle-o for the bottle shop.
Others end in IE, like brekkie, barbie, sunnies, mozzie and Chrissie.
Names get the same treatment.
A David might become Davo, a Sharon becomes Shazza, and a Barry becomes Bazza.
Many outsiders assume all this shortening comes from laziness.
But the research tells a more interesting story.
In 2011, three Australian researchers, Evan Kidd, Nenagh Kemp and Sara Quinn, published a study of these words.
They surveyed more than a hundred Australians, aged from seventeen to eighty-four.
They found that hypocoristics aren't random or sloppy at all.
They follow regular patterns, much like other ways that English builds new words.
And they're used by people of all ages and all levels of education, not just in casual pub talk.
Here's another surprise.
Many of these short words aren't actually shorter to say.
Afternoon has three syllables, and arvo has two.
But mosquito has three, and mozzie still has two.
Bottle shop is three syllables, and bottle-o is three as well.
If the point were saving effort, bottle-o would make no sense.
So what's really going on?
Linguists who study Australian English, such as Kate Burridge, have argued that these words are mainly about tone.
They signal friendliness, informality and a certain easygoing attitude.
Calling the ambulance officer an ambo makes them feel like one of us, rather than an official.
It's a bit like a verbal wink.
The words also mark you as belonging.
Using them well is a quiet way of showing you're a local.
And of course, the word Aussie itself is one of them.
Part three. Fair dinkum and the ute.
Our third expression is probably the most famous piece of Australian English of all.
Fair dinkum.
F, A, I, R.
Then D, I, N, K, U, M.
For example, I thought he was joking about winning the raffle, but it was fair dinkum.
Fair dinkum means genuine, honest, the real thing.
It can be a question, too.
If someone tells you a wild story, you might reply, fair dinkum?
That means, are you serious?
You may have heard that the word came from Chinese miners on the goldfields, supposedly saying din gum, meaning real gold.
It's a lovely story, but the evidence doesn't support it.
Dictionary researchers have found that dinkum was already a dialect word in parts of England, including Lincolnshire.
There it meant work, or a fair share of work.
Fair dinkum was used a bit like fair's fair.
The first Australian record of dinkum comes from 1888, in Rolf Boldrewood's bushranger novel Robbery Under Arms.
There, it simply means hard work.
Within a few years, fair dinkum was being used to mean honest or genuine, and it took off.
During the First World War, Australian soldiers were sometimes called dinkums, or dinkum Aussies.
Dinkum on its own still works as an adjective.
A dinkum offer is a genuine one, and a dinkum Aussie is the real deal.
Our final word is ute.
U, T, E.
For example, we threw the surfboards in the back of the ute and headed for the coast.
Ute is short for utility, and the vehicle itself is a genuine Australian invention.
The story goes that in the early 1930s, a farmer's wife in Victoria wrote to Ford Australia with a simple request.
She wanted a vehicle to go to church in on a Sunday, and which could carry the pigs to market on Monday.
A young Ford designer in Geelong called Lewis Bandt took up the challenge.
He combined the front of a comfortable car with a tray at the back.
Henry Ford himself is said to have dismissed it as a kangaroo chaser, but farmers and tradies loved it.
Ford released the coupe utility in 1934, and it became a national icon.
So how do all these words get recorded?
Australian English has its own dictionaries.
The Macquarie Dictionary was first published in 1981, and the Australian National Dictionary, put together at the Australian National University, followed in 1988.
Both track new words and hunt for the earliest examples of old ones.
That's why we can now say with some confidence where fair dinkum came from, and why the goldfields story doesn't hold up.
To sum up, Australian English grew out of a mix of British and Irish accents, blended by the children of the early colony.
Its shortened words, like arvo and servo, follow real patterns and mainly signal friendliness, not laziness.
And expressions like fair dinkum and ute each carry a genuine piece of Australian history.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did dinkum originally mean in English dialect, and in its first Australian record in 1888?
Answer. Work, or a fair share of work.
Question two. Name two common endings Australians add to shortened words.
Answer. The O ending, as in arvo and servo, and the IE ending, as in brekkie and barbie.
Question three. Where was the first coupe utility, the original ute, designed?
Answer. At Ford in Geelong, released in 1934.
That's the end of Aussie English, Explained. Good on ya. See you next arvo, or whenever suits.
